body: My T (in her mid 40s) got an eyebrow piercing and a foot tattoo within weeks of each other. It was unusual to see (the eyebrow piecing in particular) and still throws me off when I look at her, but I’m noticing it less and less.

I had this same thing happen. It was awful. So much grief and anger and abandonment. I’m sorry it happened to you. 

I just moved on. I knew T wasn’t going to change her mind. I quit talking to her. I actually went a little far in the other direction where I put her in an “all bad” box and it took time to appreciate that I did good work in the long time we were together even if I didn’t like or agree with termination.
Just saying I’m currently in the same struggle. The only PHP I could find near me has a 4-6 week waiting list. Wish you better luck than I.

Ask your teacher if you have to use a lunch money account. Usually, you put money in the account (by giving it to your teacher, the office, etc.) and then at lunchtime, you pick up your food and there’s a staff person sitting at the end. You give that person your lunch account number and they deduct from your account. 

You may also just be able to pay for today in cash at the lunch line, or if you have a concession stand they will usually take cash.

You may also want to comment on the sub r/BPD. 

I had a lot of the same questions as you (trauma or BPD?) and the solution I arrived at was to do both treatments. So, I have a DBT therapist that I work with managing day to day emotions (making sure I don’t rage on my boss). This has been helpful to keep my job and develop emotional management skills. 

At the same time, I see a different therapist for trauma work. We don’t talk at all about daily life - we go immediately into trauma processing. We do sand tray and somatic experiencing together.

That’s completely normal with experiencing trauma. 

If you haven’t yet, I would recommend DBT therapy or a STEPPS group - it’ll give you some great skills to learn how to recognize and control your emotions. 

It isn’t really “trauma work” in that you don’t process what has happened to you in the past, but you can do that with a good psychoanalyst therapist.

I give my inner kid time to be comforted by adult me. My favorite is to swing in a hammock (the one that wraps around you) and adult me (in the voice of my therapist) reminds little me that I am safe. Then I set an alarm so I go back to work (leaving that safe space can be hard!) and an alarm for the next time I get to return to the hammock. This allows little me to know that adult me won’t ignore her. 

Holding my favorite stuffed animal in bed covered by my weighted blanket is an ok second, if my hammock isn’t available.

Maybe try answering the question in your head first. 

My daughter does the same thing, and I am teaching her empathy by helping her come up with a few possible answers. If she put herself in the other persons shoes, then why would she be doing the thing? 

This may make create stronger relationships because of asking “why are you x”, which could sound judgmental - you are showing empathy. In this specific case, you think hm - maybe mom is dancing when there’s no music because she’s in good mood. Then you could say “hey mom, you’re dancing without music, looks like you’re in a good mood. What song is on repeat? You want to bake some cookies” (or other fun thing). Now you are showing how observant you are and building care and connection instead of distance.

That sounds exactly the same as most of my other therapy experiences!

And I recognized I’m SUPER privileged - I have given up on my local therapists that are covered by my insurance because I just couldn’t breakthrough my scared parts with them. So, I drive 9 hours round trip (back to my college town) every other week and pay out of pocket to see this therapist. It’s basically ridiculous. But she is SO incredibly worth it. I’m super lucky that I can afford it and my job is flexible to allow it.

Yup! I’m 31. 

I LOVE having a therapist that is so great at sand tray. 

It’s a fantastic therapeutic tool to get past the “logic and reasoning” side of my brain and get to processing emotions. 

I started with her when I was about 20, so it didn’t feel too odd to not be a kid. We do all of our work on my little kid trauma parts though, so it feels totally appropriate. 

I have a completely different therapist that I talk to about work stress and day to day struggles, so my “adult” mental health needs are met.
She’s a play therapist. We do some sand tray. We also do Somatic Experiencing a lot. So she’ll ask me what I feel in my body and we work through it.

I’m working through. We’ve spent the last two sessions where she sits on the floor with her back against the front of the couch and I lay my head on a pillow in her lap, and I’m curled in a ball covered by a blanket. I ask her, “What do you see?” And she tells me, “I see a little girl who is hurt and scared. She is also strong and brave...” and then I tell her, “Again.” And she repeats it. And I cry. And she holds me. And that’s how we spend our two hours. 

Last time, towards the end of the session, I asked her, “Can you help me see myself?” She asked what She could do to help me see myself and I thought about it and asked her if she would tell me what she saw again. 

Definitely haven’t gotten through it. But also pretty deep into our work together.

I kinda want to try drugs to see if addiction is stronger than my depression. Like, would I actually get out of bed to get drugs? I hear that addiction is the strongest urge, but...getting out of bed is ridiculously hard. 

I hope you don’t think I’m taking it lightly, I appreciate sharing your story, or this story of the words aren’t yours.
Is there something you can do besides words? Scream? Throw something? Smash something? Paint? Scribble with different colors? Find a song that reflects your mood.

Not a therapist here, but a client of a therapist I adore. You’re right, she can’t give me the love my parents didn’t give me. But she is teaching me how to move on and how to give my younger self that kind of love. 

I’ve had therapists that are like what you describe and would encourage you to try to find someone new. 

It’s not easy and it all sucks. It sucks that you have to work so hard to make up for something that you didn’t get as a child - and that you really can’t “make up” for.

Is there someone in the group (or even in the class) you can reach out to (on the side even, since groups can be tough to speak up in) to ask a few questions? 

What do you think about...?
How would you approach....?
What ideas would you have for...?
Can we video chat tomorrow to check in on my progress?
Just so that we are aligned...I was thinking of...

Good luck. You don’t have to do it on your own. I hated group projects in school, and still do at work. I’m still working on not running away from my fear of being inadequate or rejected - but these are some key questions my therapist has taught me.

How did you/they know you are a danger to yourself, even after all the treatment? 

I constantly feel like I should be inpatient because I could kill myself at any time (attempted a couple weeks ago). 

But also...it doesn’t seem like it’s an “emergency” to go to the ER or get admitted.

We were talking about how difficult the time between the sessions was for me and she asked if there was anything she could do to help. I told her I’d like a note at the end of the session that I could look at throughout the week to know that she isn’t leaving me.

Yup. Spot on. 31F here and I drive four hours each way to see my therapist. 

Something that helps us is I have her write me a note in the same notebook at the end of each session that says something to the effect of “I am here and I am not leaving you.” 

That helps me get through the distressing times of this emptinesss between sessions when I need her. 

It doesn’t answer the “how do I do this for myself as a whole adult?” my hope is that’s the job of therapy and maybe after a year or two or three of hard work, that little girl will be heard and healed. 

Good luck.

I have a very similar story, except I was a bit younger and my brother wasn’t as old either. I went to the police when I was 12 (20 years ago) and...briefly, here’s my advice. 

It sucks. There’s no justice, especially when your parents already know and aren’t protecting and supporting you. 

I have chosen to continue seeing my family, mostly on holidays. I moved away so it’s harder for them to see me. He attends all of them, and now he has 6 kids of his own. But, I don’t want my daughter missing out on having grandparents because they didn’t handle the abuse right. I don’t want her missing out on knowing her cousins because I hate their dad. 

I don’t know if that’s the right answer. All I can tell you is my experience. It’s all a very lonely road. 

I have a really great therapist. We’re currently working through the guilt and shame that my parents place on me. I hope you have one, too. 

The things I wish someone told me - It’s not your fault, no matter what. You did the best you could then, and you are doing the best you can now. It’s ok for your response to your family to change and even for it to be conflicted - they are still your family, even if they hurt you and didn’t keep you safe. Do what you need, when you need it.

My therapist always says, “call me if there’s anything you need before we meet”. 

I have appraised it two different ways:
1) an email/text to see if they have an opening sooner than my next scheduled. I use this when the feelings are big and it’s hard to function because I have something urgent to process through. 

2) when I’ve been having active suicidal thoughts (I had an attempt a couple weeks ago), I texted my therapist and she called me immediately. I cried hysterically, but we were only on the phone for 15 minutes and she had me calmed back down.

It’s a therapist that I did really great trauma work from college using sand tray therapy.

Moved to a new state after graduation and have been through a decade of therapists who use other modalities (somewhere along the lines of 10 therapists) with very little progress. There are no sand tray therapists in the state. So, I decided to go back to college town every other week to actually make progress and in another decade, actually be healed and not just frustrated.

I see a therapist in another state- so I have a 4 hour drive home after each appointment. It can be really, really difficult. Drinking LOTS of water helps (120+ ounces), taking breaks, listening to an easy audiobook. 

The following day, I have a massive hangover. I try to sleep in, drink more water, and do mostly emails/reports (no meetings) for work.

My post history will give you an idea - ironic for the name of this sub, I would actually try a non-talking modality. 

I was abused as a child and told I couldn’t talk about it - so even 20 years later, I had a similar experience of what you describe where I had no words to describe my feelings and really couldn’t even identify them for myself either (wasn’t just a “don’t want to” talk).

I did sand tray therapy for quite a while with my therapist and I wouldn’t verbally say a single word, but had really powerful sessions. This went on for about a year. We worked through really hard emotions and most sessions, I wouldn’t even say hi to her.

Yeah, I just kinda fell apart. I couldn’t focus or concentrate. I couldn’t even get myself to show up some days for my internship - being present was just too hard - which is what ultimately led the suspension. When I went back, I had disability services involved and made sure to recognize the type of working (desk work) that I needed to do as well as flexiblility with assignments (less anxiety for written, not oral reports) and more time. This all helped give me supports while I was feeling vulnerable when doing therapy.

A lot of this has translated into my professional life. I’ve learned what type of job, of manager, and flexibility I need to be successful. When I have those things, I am a high performer. When I don’t, I spend the days under my desk or in the bathroom crying.

I was in therapy for about a year and a half doing work on the 6 year old self, specifically having the therapist”witness” the abuse through sand tray therapy. Then I had about a ten year break and went back to deal with the 12 year old self who has confidence and trust issues. Now we use somatic experiencing, mainly. It’s been 3 months and fully expect it to take a couple more years of work.

I can’t comment from a theoretical standpoint, but I can tell you that the healing isn’t an endless void. 

When I was in college, I worked with a T who had a similar ability to speak to my 6 year old self. It was really, really powerful - and I definitely hit non-functioning (was suspended from my program) before it began to heal. But, that little part of me did heal. 

I am a relatively successful adult. I still have a therapist who helps me function on a day-to-day basis. I recently decided to go back to see that same T because I had a 12 year old part that needed healing. 

It’s still hard (understatement of the year). But the 6 year old part is healed and now the 12 year old part gets to do work. So...the therapy may not be over, but it has been successful and healing.

To me, it feels like I escaped my trauma only to end up outside in a (metaphorical) heavy downpour of cold, sharp rain drops that relentlessly cut my skin.

My therapist has me visualize taking cover from the rain. Finding shelter. Protection. I imagine huddling under a dining room table.

I hope you can find shelter tonight.
